Implicit Ads · theory note · November 10, 2026

Who is part of whom, and why it governs interference

Tate McRae × Adidas and Sydney Sweeney × Novig as opposite cases · public data · exploratory

An ambassador deal creates two links, not one. One runs from the celebrity to the brand: whenever people think of Tate, does Adidas come along? The other runs from the brand to the celebrity: whenever people think of Adidas, does Tate come along? How big each link is depends on how much else is already stored under each name, and that determines both what the celebrity can do for the brand and how much interference the celebrity creates.

Bottom line

  1. Tate × Adidas is a weak link, tilted slightly forward. After the July 22 campaign, Adidas appears in 0.18% of Tate's English news coverage and Tate in 0.12% of Adidas's. Neither shows up in the other's Wikipedia clicks or related searches. Both memories are crowded: Tate's with her songs and relationships, Adidas's with its founders, its rivals and eleven ambassadors. Theory says crowding at both cues caps what the deal can do.
  2. Sweeney × Novig is the backward regime. Novig had almost no public memory, so the campaign wrote it. Sweeney became 90% of Novig's news coverage and 26% of the clicks leaving its Wikipedia page, while Novig is a sliver of hers.
  3. Theory predicts opposite risks. Tate's forward link is limited by interference at her name, from her songs, tours and relationships. Sweeney's backward link creates interference inside the brand: the celebrity and the controversy crowd out the category (“sports prediction market”) that should bring Novig to mind when a bettor decides where to bet.

1. The claim

Write the public memory of an entity as everything that is written, searched and read about it. Its representation, in Sarkar's sense, is the average of those documents. Then:

Forward strength a(c→b)
share of the celebrity's memory that is the brand
“When I think of Tate, does Adidas come to mind?”
Backward strength β(b→c)
share of the brand's memory that is the celebrity
“When I think of Novig, does Sweeney come to mind?”

Our claim is that these two numbers, together with how large and crowded each memory already is, determine how a celebrity link affects interference: whether the celebrity's appearances bring the brand to mind over its rivals, and whether the celebrity takes over the brand's own cue.

2. What theory says

2.1 Ads as Cues: asymmetry is interference

In Bordalo, Burro, Gennaioli, Nacamulli & Shleifer (2025), a cue c brings to mind experience x with probability

rx(c) = S(c, x) · fx / Σx′ S(c, x′) · fx′   (their eq. 1)

Similarity S is symmetric. The numerator is association times frequency; the denominator is interference: everything else the cue also calls up, including the “fog” of unbranded experiences. Apply it to both directions of one pair with the same S(Tate, Adidas):

log rAdidas(Tate) − log rTate(Adidas) = log Σx′S(Adidas,x′)fx′ − log Σx′S(Tate,x′)fx′ + log fAdidas/fTate

So the asymmetry has two sources: how crowded each cue is (the denominators) and how familiar each target is (the frequencies). Adidas is both crowded and familiar, which makes Adidas → Tate weak. Tate → Adidas is limited instead by how crowded Tate's own memory is: her songs, tour and relationships all compete with Adidas when Tate is the cue. Novig is neither crowded nor familiar, so the backward link becomes enormous. Their Proposition 2 adds the rival channel: a cue that mostly retrieves the category raises demand for the rival the consumer already uses, more so for habitual users. Brand-specific cues avoid this.

2.2 The fan effect: one cue, many associates

Memory research finds that the more facts are attached to a concept, the more weakly each one is retrieved from it (Anderson 1974; Anderson & Reder 1999). In ACT-R the strength from cue j to item i is Sji = S − ln(fanj). In the rational-analysis version it is the log of P(i | j)/P(i). Anderson & Schooler (1991) estimated these quantities from New York Times headlines, which is what we do with GDELT and Common Crawl. Both versions are directional by construction. A brand with eleven ambassadors has a large fan, so each ambassador is weakly retrieved from it. A celebrity with one sportswear deal has a small fan in that category.

2.3 Cue competition in learning: overshadowing

When two cues are paired with an outcome, the more salient one takes most of the learned association: overshadowing and blocking in Rescorla–Wagner learning (Kamin 1969; Rescorla & Wagner 1972). In consumer learning, brand names can block learning of attribute–quality links (van Osselaer & Alba 2000; van Osselaer & Janiszewski 2001). Pairing an unknown brand with a superstar therefore makes the brand memorable, but the superstar overshadows what the brand does. Advertising research calls the endorser version the vampire effect: celebrities can reduce recall of the brand they endorse (Evans 1988; Erfgen, Zenker & Sattler 2015).

2.4 Familiar brands resist interference; endorsers can be diluted

Ads for familiar brands are less vulnerable to competitive interference than ads for unfamiliar ones (Burke & Srull 1988; Kent & Allen 1994). An endorser with many deals is a weaker cue for each (Tripp, Jensen & Carlson 1994). Meaning transfer runs from the celebrity to the product (McCracken 1989). Similarity judgments are themselves asymmetric, with the less prominent object judged more like the prominent one (Tversky 1977). In brand-equity terms, Keller (1993), these are directed links in an associative network.

Where we addAds as Cues treats similarity as symmetric and measures it from ad text. Celebrity links are directional, and their strengths can be measured from public memory, from both sides, over time. The two cases are the extremes of that variation.

Tate McRae × Adidas

The July 22 campaign barely registers in public memory. GDELT finds 2 English articles naming both, against 1,126 about Tate and 1,660 about Adidas after the campaign. Tate's Wikipedia readers go to The Kid LAROI, Cole Sillinger and her albums; Adidas's go to Adolf Dassler, Nike and Puma. A deal of this kind gives Adidas one more forward cue among many, which is the fan-effect prediction for a brand with many ambassadors.

Clearer forward-regime examples in our dataLight Common Crawl News sample: Nike is named in 14% of articles about A'ja Wilson, and she is named in none about Nike. Dior is in 9% of Anya Taylor-Joy's articles; she is in none of Dior's. In Qwen free association, LeBron James brings up Nike in 57% of samples and Kendall Jenner brings up Calvin Klein in 53%, while neither brand ever brings up the person. Any of these would make a stronger forward case alongside Sweeney × Novig.

4. Predictions

  • Implicit-ad value scales with forward strength. When the celebrity is in the news for unrelated reasons (a tour, a film, a breakup), the brand should get a lift proportional to a(c→b). Tate: positive but bounded by her crowded memory (songs, The Kid LAROI, tour). Sweeney: near zero for Novig outside the ad itself.
  • Contagion scales with backward strength. Shocks to the celebrity should move the brand in proportion to β(b→c). Sweeney news should move Novig search; Tate news should not move Adidas.
  • Fan effect on the brand side. Each additional ambassador should be a smaller share of the brand's memory, while each still adds a forward channel. Big brands buy a portfolio of forward cues; they do not let any one person redefine them.
  • Overshadowing of the category for young brands. With high β, the link from the category to the brand (“sports prediction market” → Novig) should grow more slowly than attention to the brand. That category → brand link is the cue that matters when a bettor decides where to bet.
  • Rival spillover depends on familiarity and specificity. Category-heavy ads for unfamiliar brands help familiar rivals among habitual users (Ads as Cues, Prop. 2). A celebrity with strong forward strength to one brand is a brand-specific cue, which limits that spillover.
